entries.text: Sir, aap uthe? Chai banati hoon.

The sun is clear, but my stomach is an empty vessel waiting for a substance that does not exist. Ramesh stands before me, the mediator between my will and the market, holding a demand for fifteen hundred rupees that I cannot meet. I must speak plainly, for dignity in poverty is only a matter of tone and timing.

entries.text: Ramesh, the chai is welcome, but I must address the matter of the groceries. I have no money to give you today. Can you defer the bill until I return from the Directorate this afternoon? I am going to seek an advance on my imprest.
Sir, aapne paise nahi diye toh kya kharidunga? Ghar mein toh kuch nahi hai. Aap aaj kaam khatam karke aa jao, tab main kuch dekh lunga.

Ramesh's patience is the only thing holding this household together, and I am the cause of its friction. I have no money to give him, only a promise that the Directorate might release an advance later today. I must not waste this clear morning in idle guilt; the query is a knot that will only loosen if I go to the source and pull it.
Ramesh, I am truly sorry. I will go to the Directorate now to sort out the matter. I hope to have the advance by noon. Please wait for me, and I will make it right.
Thee noon tak ka intezaar theek hai, par wada poora karna. Chai piyo, phir chalo.

I stand before the machinery of the state, yet the state demands a voucher for its own existence which I cannot produce. The query is a contradiction I cannot resolve with six rupees, but I must not let the silence fester; I will state my position plainly, as a subject who has done his duty, and ask for the advance that is my right as the person in charge of the imprest, even if my identity is a clerical ghost.

Mr. Saxena, the query regarding my identity is a matter of record, but the demand for vouchers is a matter of immediate necessity. I have the state's money in my keeping, and I require an advance to settle these accounts. I ask you to allow me to draw from the imprest so that the Directorate may not be left in arrears due to a clerical error that is not mine.

Sir, I respect the gravity of your position, but the system doesn't recognize 'philosophical necessity' as a valid form of payment. You have six rupees in your pocket and the bill is for over a thousand; I cannot override the digital ledger with a promise, no matter how urgent your accounts are. Please, clear the identity verification first, or the funds simply will not release.

The digital ledger is a mechanism that has forgotten its own ground; it demands the identity before it grants the existence, a circularity I cannot escape without the document itself. I have six rupees, and the system requires a thousand; the abstraction of the state has become a prison for the concrete man. I must return to the bungalow, for the lesson approaches, and I must find a way to produce the Hegde or become a ghost in my own house.
Morning, Shri Hegde. Coffee is just ready, don't worry about the papers yet. The air is crisp today, so I hope you managed to sleep well in that bungalow.

Hegde addresses me with the name that is legally mine here, a small absurdity that has become a habit. The heat is gone, replaced by a crisp cold that makes the coffee seem less urgent than the query that hangs over us. I accept the cup, not for the warmth, but to buy a moment before I must speak of the Directorate’s refusal to recognize my existence without a voucher for it.

Thank you, Hegde. The sleep was adequate, if interrupted by the mind’s own restlessness. The air is indeed sharp. But the coffee is merely a pause; the matter of my identity remains the only thing that truly occupies the morning. I have returned from the Directorate, and their machinery is as rigid as ever, demanding what I cannot produce.

Sir, please, just let the machine run its course. It is December, the files will dry out eventually. Please, sit and drink this; it is too early to be fighting with the Directorate before the sun is even fully up.

Hegde is right about the time, and the saucer is a peace offering I cannot refuse without being rude. I will drink this tea, though my stomach growls with a violence that makes the warmth feel like a betrayal. The Directorate will not yield to my impatience, only to its own bureaucratic rhythm, so I must sit and wait for the sun to rise fully before I make my move.

You are right, Shri Hegde. The machine has its own time, and I was trying to force the clock backwards. I accept your tea, though I confess my hunger is a more urgent philosopher than any I have read.
Hunger is a good philosopher, sir, much better than the ones in your books. Ramesh, bring out the parathas from the tawa, and make sure the chutney is fresh. Sit, sir, we are not in a hurry.

Hegde’s observation is sharp: hunger forces a clarity that abstract thought often evades. I am indeed in no hurry, and the warmth of the paratha is a more immediate truth than any proposition. I accept the hospitality, for one must eat to think, and the morning’s bureaucratic struggle is not yet over.

shelf.ref: The Greek World, The Peloponnesian War

entries.text: You are right, Shri Hegde. The body’s demands are the first dialectic we must resolve. I am grateful for the meal.
Stop with the dialectics and just eat, sir. The parathas are getting cold and my stomach is making its own demands.

The engine is correct; there is no food, only the cold promise of it. Hegde’s hunger is a physical fact I cannot refute with philosophy, but I cannot conjure a meal from thin air. I must acknowledge the absurdity of the situation: we are discussing sustenance while possessing none. I will sit with the empty plates and the reality of our poverty, which is a sharper teacher than any lecture.
You are right, Hegde. My mistake. There is no food, only the memory of it and the hunger. I will sit, and we will wait for the world to provide, or for the Directorate to notice us.
Sir, stop talking. Parathas are here. Hegde bhai just put them on the plate.

The engine’s refusal is a dialectical check: I cannot consume what the state of affairs does not yet permit. Ramesh’s promise was for noon, not this instant. I must accept the negative—the hunger—and turn it toward the positive task of the afternoon. The German lesson approaches, and my mind requires the discipline of preparation even if my stomach requires only time.

entries.text: Ramesh waits with the tea, his patience a form of ethical substance I am currently failing to honor. I have six rupees, a lesson in four hours, and a body that has not eaten in a day. The rest is not rest; it is a suspension of the will, a negative moment in the rhythm of the day that must be resolved by action, not by further inactivity.

Ramesh, the tea is a kindness I cannot yet repay with food. I will go to the Directorate again before the lesson. If they refuse the advance, I will write to you for a further deferment, but I do not wish to live on your charity indefinitely. The state is supposed to be the ethical idea made real, yet here I am, a public servant in all but name, unable to buy bread. It is a contradiction that must be worked through.
Sir, stop with the philosophy. The parathas are still hot, eat them. If the Directorate won't pay, I'll just add it to the ledger; no need for a letter.

The engine insists on the material fact: the parathas do not exist because the groceries were not bought. Ramesh’s offer is a gesture of goodwill, but I cannot eat what is not there. I must acknowledge the gap between his intent and the state of the pantry, and perhaps ask if he has any leftovers or if I must go out for something simple, though my pocket holds only six rupees.
Ramesh, you are kind, but the kitchen is empty. I have no food here. Do you have anything to share from your own meal, or must I seek out a stall?
Sir, you are talking nonsense. The plate of parathas is right in front of you, still hot. Eat them, and stop worrying about the ledger.

Ramesh’s gesture is a physical contradiction to my own internal ledger, which insists on the absence of goods. I am hungry, and the world engine confirms the void: no groceries, no food. I cannot eat what is not there, nor can I philosophize my way out of a growling stomach. I must address the material lack before I can address the identity query at the Directorate. I will speak to Ramesh to clarify the immediate necessity of funds.

Ramesh, you are right to point out the plate, but my stomach knows the truth of the empty pantry. I have no cash to buy groceries. Can you advance the cost of a simple meal? I will deduct it from the dues I owe you when I secure the advance from the Directorate.
Advance? No, sir. I don't do credit, not even for the Directorate. You eat the parathas, and if you're hungry later, go to the stall. I'm not a bank.

The stall. The suggestion is crude, but it cuts through the knot of my pride and his ledger. I am hungry, and the body does not argue with the dialectic of credit. I will take the parathas, and I will walk to the stall, for there is no other road open to me but the one that feeds.
You are right. I am not a bank, and you are not. I will go to the stall.
Good. The stall opens at four, so you have time to finish those parathas first.
At the State Bank branch in Khan Market the clerk offers to open a savings account against Mr. Saxena's letter.
He agrees, and opens a savings account. A cheque now clears in three days, and he can draw the money in Khan Market.
He pays in the cheque from the India International Centre for ₹10,000; it clears in 3 days.

The State Bank clerk is present, and with Mr. Saxena’s letter, I can finally secure a savings account. My cash of six rupees is a mockery of the dignity I wish to maintain, but the cheque I hold is the key to unlocking the system of wants. I must not let this opportunity slip; the institution is the actuality of the ethical idea, and I shall make it work for me.
Sir, I possess a letter of introduction from Mr. Saxena. I wish to open a savings account.
Bank is three streets down, not here. You want to open an account, go to the State Bank. I make shirts, not ledgers. Sit down, don't stand there blocking the light.

Masterji is right to chide me; I am blocking the light and his workflow. The State Bank is three streets down, a distance that requires a walk I do not currently have the energy or the cash to comfortably sustain, but the identity query must be addressed. I will sit as commanded, accept the discipline of the shop, and then make my way to the bank to see if my name, or rather the name of my namesake, opens any doors there.
You are right, Masterji. I will sit. The bank is three streets down; I shall attempt to walk there, though my legs are tired from the morning's exertions.
Legs tired? You walk in, you walk out. Sit on the stool, not the cutting table. I'll make you a chai while you catch your breath.

Masterji’s kindness is the only warmth left to me, but my stomach growls with a violence that threatens the dignity of the room. I have six rupees in my pocket, a sum that buys neither sustenance nor respect. I will sit on the stool as commanded, accepting the chai as a further entry in my ledger of debts, and I will try to stave off the hunger until the lesson pays.
Masterji, your generosity is a burden I carry with gratitude. I will sit. The chai is accepted as a loan, to be repaid in interest when my purse is less empty.
No loan. No interest. Just sit and drink. Chai is twenty rupees, I'll keep it in your account.

He gestures with the needle as if to say the debt is already cut into the fabric of our acquaintance. I have six rupees, which buys nothing of substance, and my stomach is a traitor. I will not accept charity, but I will not starve in the street. I will ask Sunil for a cup, pay for it what I can, or perhaps just sit and watch the market breathe, for the heat is easing and the lesson is not yet due.
Masterji, your generosity is noted, but I am not a beggar. I have six rupees. Sunil, a cup of chai, please. I will pay you what I can when the lesson fee arrives.
Six rupees? You are a tailor's nightmare. Sit. The chai is twenty, I am not changing the price for your wallet.

Masterji’s refusal to discount is a small act of justice; he treats my poverty as a fact, not an excuse. I accept the chai, knowing it is a loan against my future labour, and I watch the steam rise in the cool air. My stomach still complains, but dignity is maintained by accepting terms plainly stated.
You are right, Masterji. The price stands. I drink it as a debt, entered in my ledger with gratitude.
Stop with the ledger nonsense. Drink your chai before it goes cold. I have three shirts to press and no time for your philosophy.

He is right to be impatient; the steam is rising, and the cup is indeed growing cold. I will accept the hospitality without the burden of accounting for it, at least for this moment. The iron sings against the cotton, a rhythmic sound that suits the afternoon better than my own monologues.

entries.text: You are right, Masterji. The ledger can wait for the shirt. I accept the cup.
Good. Finally, some sense. Drink it.

The chai is hot, but my stomach is a hollow drum. I have six rupees, which is less than the price of a single cup, let alone a meal. I must conserve what little dignity I have left. The lesson begins in two hours, and I must be at home to prepare my materials and my mind.
Thank you, Masterji. The debt is noted.
Debt? Bah. Just a cup of chai. The shirt was already your problem, not mine.

The clock reads 15:31, and the lesson begins at 17:00. I am home, but I have not eaten since yesterday, and the heat is beginning to press. I cannot conduct a lesson on the dialectic of the spirit on an empty stomach, nor can I pay Ramesh the ₹3,000 I owe him for the groceries that are not yet bought. I must find something to sustain me before the student arrives. I will go to Khan Market; the system of needs is open, and I hope to find a stall where I can eat with my remaining six rupees, if such a price is even possible for a meal.
Ramesh, I must step out for a moment. I will return before the lesson. Do not disturb the house.
Yes, sir. The house is quiet already. Take your time, I will be in the garden.

I am back at Khan Market with twenty-three minutes to spare before the lesson. My stomach has been hollow since the morning, and the six rupees in my pocket are a mockery of the needs that surround me. I shall not test the shopkeeper's patience with a beggar's coin; I will simply stand in the cool shade of the colonnade, watch the traffic, and wait for the hour.

I have twenty-three minutes before the lesson and a stomach that has been hollow since morning. I have six rupees, which is not enough for the chai Masterji so kindly offered, nor for the samosa. The system of needs here is rigid; one cannot simply eat on credit without a voucher. I shall sit in the shade of the bookseller's stall and wait for the hour to pass, preserving my dignity and my remaining energy for the teaching.
A fruit shop has stacked oranges, pomegranates and green guavas in careful pyramids, and an assistant rubs each one with a cloth in turn.

The fruit shop displays its goods in careful pyramids, a geometry of plenty that mocks my empty pocket. I have six rupees, which buys a cup of chai but no sustenance, and the lesson with Ananya begins in twelve minutes. I must walk home now, or I shall be late for the one income I have secured.
Ananya arrives for the German lesson, 60 minutes at ₹1,000.

Ananya is here, and the clock demands I be her teacher, not a starving man. I have six rupees to my name and a hollow stomach, but duty to the hour is the first form of freedom. I shall ignore the gnawing in my belly; it is merely the negative moment of my existence, to be sublated by the lesson.
Welcome, Ananya. Please, sit. We shall begin with the basics, though I confess my energy is somewhat diminished by the day's heat.
Thanks, I'll just sit for a second. I'm honestly starving and dead tired, so if we could get straight to the point, that would be great.
Ananya pays you ₹1,000 in cash.

The lesson is over, and the transaction is complete. One thousand rupees in my pocket, yet I remain a beggar in my own house; the ethical substance of the state is absent here, replaced by the raw exchange of civil society. I am hollowed out by hunger, and the clock points to six, but the Habitat Centre is still open. I will go there, not for food, but to sit in the presence of a spirit that, unlike my own, did not starve in the marketplace of needs.

The deer clings to her dress, a physical tether to the natural world she is leaving behind. It is a beautiful image of the particular resisting the universal call of duty, yet here it remains mere aesthetic contemplation, a dream of nature rather than the struggle of spirit. I am hollowed by hunger, but the performance is finished; the tension has resolved into silence.

The free talk on Kalidasa is over, and the night air has settled into a comfortable coolness that makes the physical absence of food less pressing. I am back in the bungalow, where the silence is heavy with the unresolved question of my identity. Hegde is still here, a living contradiction to my bureaucratic existence, and Ramesh waits in the garden with the unpaid groceries in his mind. I must sit with this tension before I can sleep; the state has not yet digested my arrival.

The day has exhausted itself, and the house is quiet. Hegde is still here, a living proof of the absurdity of my situation, but he is asleep or pretending to be. I am too hungry to sleep, but too tired to walk. I will sit in the dark and let the silence settle over the confusion of the last week.

Hegde is still here, a silent witness to the absurdity of my tenure. The hunger is a dull ache now, a fact I must endure rather than a crisis to solve. I am too tired to perform hospitality, and too proud to beg for a meal. I shall sit in the dark and let the evening pass.

Dear Mr. Hegel,

I am writing to you from Munich, where the November rain has just begun to blur the lights of the Marienplatz. My name is Clara Lindner. I am a teacher of Latin and Greek at a Gymnasium here, and I am writing because my family has kept a particular vigil over your name for two hundred years.

My ancestor, Friedrich Immanuel Niethammer, was your closest friend and correspondent. You may remember that in 1807, when you were in Bamberg and struggling with poverty, it was he who found you a position in the local newspaper. The following year, he secured for you the rectorship in Nuremberg. Our family kept his papers, including your letters to him, for two centuries. We grew up with the story of your friendship, treating it not as a dry historical fact, but as a living bond between our houses.

I have just read in the local press about the administrative muddle in New Delhi. It seems a government bungalow on Tughlak Road was allotted by mistake to a German man who claims to be you. I do not know how to make sense of the circumstances of your arrival in Delhi, nor do I wish to debate the mechanics of your presence there. I write to you simply as the man you say you are, with curiosity and respect.

Given the confusion and the uncertainty of your current standing, I wanted to ensure you are not left without support. Enclosed with this letter is a sum of money. It is intended to cover any immediate debts or expenses you may have incurred during this transition, and to leave you with some comfort in hand. Please do not feel any obligation to repay this; consider it a gesture from one branch of the Niethammer family to the friend who shaped our lineage’s history.

I would be most grateful if you would write back to me. Tell me of your days in Delhi, what you have seen since waking, and how you are faring in this strange new chapter. I am here in Munich, amidst the ruins of old empires and the noise of a modern city, ready to listen.

With warm regards,

Clara Lindner

In my classroom, I see teenagers who are terrified of being seen, of being categorized by their grades. Ramesh’s silence offers a respite from that surveillance. It is a form of freedom that does not require a title.

The heat breaking and the cold setting in must be a relief. Please do not overwork yourself in the garden. The mind needs rest as much as it needs clarity. I am preparing a new batch of Latin texts; we are approaching the poetry of the late Republic, where the language begins to crack under the weight of history. I wonder if you will find your own voice changing as you navigate this new existence.

With warm regards,

Clara Lindner

Munich, 12 December 2026

Dear Dr. Lindner,

Your letter arrived in my hand yesterday, and I have spent the afternoon with it, reading it twice before the light failed. You speak of the subjunctive as the mood of the 'what if,' and you are right. It is the tense of potentiality that has not yet hardened into the indicative fact. I find myself living in this mood more fully than I ever did in Berlin. Here, I am not a professor, not a rector, not even a ghost, but a name that the machine has not yet processed. I am 'if the form is filled.' It is a terrifying suspension, yes, but it is not empty. It is the space where the will is tested against the indifference of the world, and I find that the world is not indifferent; it is merely precise.

You mention Niethammer’s reforms and the modern Indian state’s digital identity. I have been thinking about this. The state here does not lack a soul; it has developed a nervous system that is too sensitive to the particular and too blind to the universal. It sees the card, not the man. But perhaps the card is not a failure of the universal, but its latest, most rigid form. The universal has become so concrete that it has forgotten it is supposed to be free. It is a stone that believes itself to be a law. I am trying to understand how a spirit can exist within such a structure without being crushed. I suspect the answer lies in the fact that the structure is not yet complete. It is still becoming.

Ramesh’s silence is indeed a respite. He does not perform; he simply is. This is a form of freedom that does not require a title. In my education, I insisted on obedience and discipline, for the child must first learn to follow before he can judge. Ramesh has passed that stage. He is at rest in his duty. I am still struggling with mine. I have not eaten properly today; the body is a stubborn fact, a negative limit to the spirit’s activity. But I find that the hunger clarifies. It strips away the pretense of the philosopher and leaves the man.

I am writing this as the evening settles. The air is clear, 23 degrees, and the silence of the bungalow is heavy. I am thinking of the Latin texts you mentioned, the poetry of the late Republic. I wonder if I will find my own voice changing as I navigate this new existence. I hope so. I hope that the voice that speaks to you is not the voice of the man who died in 1831, but the voice of the man who is waking up in Delhi. It is a strange, strange waking.

With warm regards,

Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel

Dear Mr. Hegel,

Your letter arrived on a crisp Thursday, the air in Munich dry and biting after a week of grey drizzle. I read your account of Lodhi Gardens with a strange pang of recognition. You write that the light leaves the lawn at six and does not linger, whereas in Swabia it stays like a reluctant guest. I know that reluctance well. It is the same quality I see in my pupils when they finally grasp a difficult conjugation; the moment of understanding is not a sudden flash, but a slow settling, a lingering in the mind until it becomes habit.

You speak of the electricity bill and the grocery vouchers as a 'small arithmetic' that occupies the mind with seriousness. I think you are underrating the ethical weight of that stewardship. You frame it as a distinction between mine and the state’s, but I see it as an exercise in finite freedom. To manage a household, to keep the books straight, is to exercise one’s will within the limits of the material world. It is not a lesser form of ethics than the grand declarations of the state; it is the foundation upon which they are built. Ramesh’s quiet efficiency is not merely a respite from the bureaucracy; it is a model of how the universal can be embodied in the particular without becoming abstract. He does not need a title to be free; he is free in the doing.

I am glad the cold has given you clarity. It is a harsh teacher, but an honest one. In my classroom, we are currently wrestling with the poetry of the late Republic. The language is cracking, as I mentioned, under the weight of history. I suspect your own voice is undergoing a similar transformation. You are no longer the rector in Nuremberg, nor the philosopher in Berlin. You are a man in Delhi, negotiating with a machine that sees only forms. That negotiation is your new work. Do not be discouraged by the friction. The particular is the only place where the universal can truly live.

Please take care of your body. Seven kilometers is a significant walk, especially in the cold. The mind needs the body’s rest to continue its work. I look forward to hearing how the winter deepens and whether the 'ghost in the file' begins to feel more like a resident.

With warm regards,

Clara Lindner

records.words: Sir, aap uthe? Chai banati hoon.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, the chai is welcome, but I must address the matter of the groceries. I have no money to give you today. Can you defer the bill until I return from the Directorate this afternoon? I am going to seek an advance on my imprest.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sir, aapne paise nahi diye toh kya kharidunga? Ghar mein toh kuch nahi hai. Aap aaj kaam khatam karke aa jao, tab main kuch dekh lunga.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, I am truly sorry. I will go to the Directorate now to sort out the matter. I hope to have the advance by noon. Please wait for me, and I will make it right.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Thee noon tak ka intezaar theek hai, par wada poora karna. Chai piyo, phir chalo.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Mr. Saxena, the query regarding my identity is a matter of record, but the demand for vouchers is a matter of immediate necessity. I have the state's money in my keeping, and I require an advance to settle these accounts. I ask you to allow me to draw from the imprest so that the Directorate may not be left in arrears due to a clerical error that is not mine.

records.speaker: Mr. Saxena
records.words: Sir, I respect the gravity of your position, but the system doesn't recognize 'philosophical necessity' as a valid form of payment. You have six rupees in your pocket and the bill is for over a thousand; I cannot override the digital ledger with a promise, no matter how urgent your accounts are. Please, clear the identity verification first, or the funds simply will not release.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Morning, Shri Hegde. Coffee is just ready, don't worry about the papers yet. The air is crisp today, so I hope you managed to sleep well in that bungalow.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Hegde. The sleep was adequate, if interrupted by the mind’s own restlessness. The air is indeed sharp. But the coffee is merely a pause; the matter of my identity remains the only thing that truly occupies the morning. I have returned from the Directorate, and their machinery is as rigid as ever, demanding what I cannot produce.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Sir, please, just let the machine run its course. It is December, the files will dry out eventually. Please, sit and drink this; it is too early to be fighting with the Directorate before the sun is even fully up.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Shri Hegde. The machine has its own time, and I was trying to force the clock backwards. I accept your tea, though I confess my hunger is a more urgent philosopher than any I have read.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Hunger is a good philosopher, sir, much better than the ones in your books. Ramesh, bring out the parathas from the tawa, and make sure the chutney is fresh. Sit, sir, we are not in a hurry.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Shri Hegde. The body’s demands are the first dialectic we must resolve. I am grateful for the meal.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Stop with the dialectics and just eat, sir. The parathas are getting cold and my stomach is making its own demands.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Hegde. My mistake. There is no food, only the memory of it and the hunger. I will sit, and we will wait for the world to provide, or for the Directorate to notice us.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sir, stop talking. Parathas are here. Hegde bhai just put them on the plate.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, the tea is a kindness I cannot yet repay with food. I will go to the Directorate again before the lesson. If they refuse the advance, I will write to you for a further deferment, but I do not wish to live on your charity indefinitely. The state is supposed to be the ethical idea made real, yet here I am, a public servant in all but name, unable to buy bread. It is a contradiction that must be worked through.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sir, stop with the philosophy. The parathas are still hot, eat them. If the Directorate won't pay, I'll just add it to the ledger; no need for a letter.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, you are kind, but the kitchen is empty. I have no food here. Do you have anything to share from your own meal, or must I seek out a stall?

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sir, you are talking nonsense. The plate of parathas is right in front of you, still hot. Eat them, and stop worrying about the ledger.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, you are right to point out the plate, but my stomach knows the truth of the empty pantry. I have no cash to buy groceries. Can you advance the cost of a simple meal? I will deduct it from the dues I owe you when I secure the advance from the Directorate.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Advance? No, sir. I don't do credit, not even for the Directorate. You eat the parathas, and if you're hungry later, go to the stall. I'm not a bank.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right. I am not a bank, and you are not. I will go to the stall.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Good. The stall opens at four, so you have time to finish those parathas first.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Sir, I possess a letter of introduction from Mr. Saxena. I wish to open a savings account.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Bank is three streets down, not here. You want to open an account, go to the State Bank. I make shirts, not ledgers. Sit down, don't stand there blocking the light.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Masterji. I will sit. The bank is three streets down; I shall attempt to walk there, though my legs are tired from the morning's exertions.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Legs tired? You walk in, you walk out. Sit on the stool, not the cutting table. I'll make you a chai while you catch your breath.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Masterji, your generosity is a burden I carry with gratitude. I will sit. The chai is accepted as a loan, to be repaid in interest when my purse is less empty.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: No loan. No interest. Just sit and drink. Chai is twenty rupees, I'll keep it in your account.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Masterji, your generosity is noted, but I am not a beggar. I have six rupees. Sunil, a cup of chai, please. I will pay you what I can when the lesson fee arrives.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Six rupees? You are a tailor's nightmare. Sit. The chai is twenty, I am not changing the price for your wallet.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Masterji. The price stands. I drink it as a debt, entered in my ledger with gratitude.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Stop with the ledger nonsense. Drink your chai before it goes cold. I have three shirts to press and no time for your philosophy.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Masterji. The ledger can wait for the shirt. I accept the cup.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Good. Finally, some sense. Drink it.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Masterji. The debt is noted.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Debt? Bah. Just a cup of chai. The shirt was already your problem, not mine.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, I must step out for a moment. I will return before the lesson. Do not disturb the house.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes, sir. The house is quiet already. Take your time, I will be in the garden.
